paper_title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

These requirements extend beyond synthesizing an isolated clip: user may change direction during walking, request an upperbody action, or specify future target while the current motion is still being executed. The resulting references must be available quickly enough for interactive use and remain compatible with downstream tracking system. Unlike offline text-to-motion synthesis, the future instruction sequence need not be known when generation begins. An interactive generator must therefore preserve useful context SUBMITTED TO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 2 Fig. 2: Interactive motion generation with Motion Mamba 2.0. Text instructions specify the requested actions, while spatial controls constrain root motion and selected joint positions. From left to right, the panels show root trajectories, root waypoints, full-body pose sequences, and selected joint positions. Blue-to-gray poses indicate temporal progression, while red overlays visualize trajectories, waypoints, and joint locations. The panels show Viser motion references and rollout tracked with SONIC. while incorporating newly arriving commands, rather than simply replaying completed trajectory. Diffusion models produce diverse text-conditioned human motion [1], [2], [3]. Recent methods extend this formulation through temporal composition, autoregressive prediction, and direct spatial conditioning [4], [5], [6], [7]. Temporal composition allows multiple descriptions to define longer sequence, while causal latent models and hierarchical motion tokens support incremental synthesis [8], [9]. Spatially constrained methods further specify where selected joints or the character should move [7], [10], [11], [12]. In particular, generating one window at time provides practical interface for online instructions. However, two difficulties remain closely connected. bounded attention cache discards older motion features, whereas an unbounded cache increases storage and computation as the sequence grows. Moreover, repeated denoising of short windows can incur substantial execution overhead even when each individual model evaluation is small. An interactive system therefore requires both suitable representation of motion history and an efficient implementation of its repeated updates. These requirements concern different aspects of the problem: reducing the number of sampling steps does not extend the history available to the model, and compact historical state alone does not eliminate denoising overhead. State-space models provide an alternative to storing every historical token by summarizing sequence in recurrent state [13], [14]. Their use in motion generation has shown the value of efficient temporal modeling [15], [16]. Recent studies also combine Mamba with autoregressive diffusion or use recurrent temporal representations for sustained and interactive motion [17], [18], [19]. Nevertheless, compressed recurrent state and an attention cache expose history differently: the former carries evolving context, while the latter permits direct retrieval of explicit features. Simply placing both branches in network does not make the recurrent history directly accessible to attention. This distinction motivates learned interface between accumulated recurrent motion state and attention-accessible content, rather than relying on either mechanism alone. Diffusion introduces an additional requirement: successive noisy candidates describe alternatives for the same output window, not successive moments of the accepted motion stream. Persisting those intermediate candidates would mix sampling iterations with physical time. We therefore treat the boundary between prediction and history commitment as part of the models streaming formulation. We propose Motion Mamba 2.0, an autoregressive diffusion model for long-horizon, real-time controllable G1 motion. The model follows rootbody decomposition [7]: explicit root predictions determine local trajectory features for body generation. Within both denoisers, local attention is combined with resumable Mamba branch. Our persistent content memory (PCM) learns to map compressed Mamba state summaries, successive state changes, and text-conditioned features into dynamically updated slots accessible to local attention. The slots complement recent motion features in the bounded cache and aim to support terminal spatial constraint satisfaction and commandconditioned generation over extended rollouts; they are not designed to reproduce arbitrary early instructions verbatim. Recurrent states, cached features, and slots are committed only after clean motion window is accepted; intermediate denoising candidates read the same immutable history snapshot. The fixed-size recurrent state, cache, and PCM slots bound stored context without guaranteeing retention of every detail from arbitrarily distant motion. The acceptedhistory separation also guides efficient inference. Readonly denoising avoids materializing unused state proposals, selective fusion reduces intermediate memory traffic, and CUDA Graphs reduce repeated host dispatch [20], [21]. These changes preserve root-to-body ordering and the canonical clean-history update. Our objective is to accelerate the same sampling computation, complementing methods that SUBMITTED TO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE obtain faster generation through compact representations or altered sampling procedures [3], [22], [23]. We measure their contributions separately, since the effect of local fusion differs from that of graph replay. The complete scheme generates 52-frame window in 276.14 ms at the median on an RTX 4090; this steady-state generation time is distinct from the delay between user command and its visible execution. We evaluate the method on three G1 motion benchmarks under matched 100,000-update training budget (App. C). We first examine shortand long-horizon generation on retargeted HiPHI [24], followed by short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed [25] and retargeted HumanML3D [26]; BONES Seed retains its officially provided G1 trajectories. The results demonstrate accurate control over extended rollouts together with strong short-horizon performance, while architectural ablations examine the contributions of recurrent state and history-dependent content memory. Finally, we conduct realworld evaluation on physical Unitree G1, which demonstrates sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We propose Motion Mamba 2.0, Mamba-based autoregressive diffusion model with persistent content memory, connecting accepted recurrent history to local attention for long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation. We develop and evaluate state-preserving inference optimizations for this architecture, combining execution-flow simplification, fusion kernel, and CUDA Graph replay. On an RTX 4090, the complete optimization achieves 6.138 median paired speedup. We evaluate the proposed framework on physical Unitree G1 through multi-stage text-guided action composition and interactive keyboard/mouse control, demonstrating continuous motion execution under changing instructions and spatial commands. The system achieves 94% full-task success across 100 trials without observed falls. preliminary version of this work appeared in our ECCV 2024 conference paper, Motion Mamba [15]. The present manuscript substantially extends the conference version in both methodology and experimental evaluation in the following six aspects. (1) We reformulate the original text-conditioned latent diffusion framework into an autoregressive rootbody diffusion architecture for long-horizon humanoid motion generation. Instead of synthesizing motion sequence as single clip, the new framework generates successive 52-frame windows while accommodating changing text instructions and time-indexed spatial constraints. (2) We redesign the temporal modeling architecture beyond the original Hierarchical Temporal Mamba (HTM) and Bidirectional Spatial Mamba (BSM) blocks. The new denoisers integrate resumable Mamba-3 recurrence with local attention and persistent content memory (PCM). PCM converts accepted recurrent-state summaries and their changes into gated content slots, providing attentionaccessible representations of compressed motion history alongside the sliding cache. (3) We introduce an acceptedonly history update mechanism for autoregressive diffusion. Intermediate noisy predictions read an immutable historical snapshot, whereas the attention cache, recurrent states, and PCM slots are updated together only after clean motion window is accepted. This separates diffusion sampling iterations from the temporal evolution of generated motion. (4) We develop hardware-aware inference pipeline that combines execution-flow simplification, custom fused kernel and CUDA Graph replay across three guidance branches. (5) We extend the evaluation from the original HumanML3D and KIT-ML text-to-motion benchmarks to unified G1 motion setting involving retargeted HiPHI, BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D. The new protocol evaluates spatial controllability, instruction matching, motion quality, and inference efficiency over autoregressive rollouts of up to 39.52 s. (6) We further extend our evaluation to physicsbased simulation and real-world deployment on Unitree G1 humanoid, assessing multi-stage text-guided actions alongside interactive spatial control via keyboard and mouse.

2 RELATED WORK
2.1 Efficient Long-Horizon Motion Generation
sections.content: Text-conditioned diffusion models learn expressive motion distributions from paired language and motion data [1], [2], [3]. Their representations and sampling procedures determine both the cost of synthesis and how motion can be extended in time. Discrete motion representations offer complementary formulation, with autoregressive token prediction in T2M-GPT [27] and masked token completion in MMM [28]. Longer sequences can be constructed by composing action-conditioned segments, extending textual context, or refining overlapping motion intervals [4], [29], [30], [31], [32], [33]. Past-conditioned diffusion and temporal motion fields further address continuity beyond isolated clips [34], [35], [36]. In particular, Lagrangian Motion Fields represent longer sequences through compact supermotions, whereas FlowMDM blends positional encodings to improve transitions between described segments [4], [36]. These approaches make temporal composition more flexible, but an interactive application additionally requires new conditions to affect stream that has already begun. Autoregressive diffusion and accelerated sampling support incremental synthesis with lower per-update cost [5], [6], [22], [23], [37]. Recent streaming methods introduce causal representations, historical context, or spatial conditioning to accommodate continuous generation [7], [8], [38], [39]. MOGO instead uses hierarchical causal Transformer over quantized motion tokens for real-time, extended generation [9]. These developments show that motion representation, temporal factorization, and sampling efficiency offer complementary routes to reducing generation cost. Controllability introduces further requirement: trajectory and joint targets must influence future motion while preserving the current action. Guided Motion Diffusion incorporates spatial constraints through representation design and diffusion guidance [10], while OmniControl combines spatial and realism guidance to constrain different joints at different times [11]. COMET studies extended joint targets for long-term generation, while ARDY exposes text and flexible kinematic constraints through hybrid SUBMITTED TO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 4 representation [7], [12]. We build on ARDYs explicit-root and latent-body representation to study how recurrent state, bounded attention, and persistent content can be integrated into its denoising process. The accompanying execution optimizations target repeated inference while preserving the architectures sampling and history-update semantics. For controlled comparison, all methods use independently trained G1 adaptations with the same 100,000-update budget; none uses its original pretrained release. 2.2 State-Space Models for Motion Structured state-space models connect recurrent, convolutional, and continuous-time sequence processing [40], [41], [42], [43]. Mamba introduces input-dependent state updates, and subsequent models extend selective scanning to visual and multidimensional data [13], [44], [45], [46]. Mamba-2 connects structured state-space models with attention through state-space duality [47]. Mamba-3 improves the underlying sequence model through state-space discretization and rotary dynamics [14]. We use this scan as temporal modeling component; its recurrence is not contribution of this work. In motion generation, state-space models have been applied to temporal and spatial dependencies, hybrid architectures, and text-conditioned synthesis [15], [16], [18], [48]. Memory-oriented variants also consider longer sequences and the retention of earlier context [49], [50]. MADM combines Mamba with autoregressive diffusion for text-tomotion generation, while Dyadic Mamba and InterMamba extend state-space modeling to interactions between people [17], [19], [51]. Cross-segment memory has also been studied in sequence models: Transformer-XL reuses earlier hidden representations through segment-level recurrence [52], while Recurrent Memory Transformer propagates dedicated memory tokens between segments [53]. Our focus is the interface between compressed recurrent motion state and attention during autoregressive diffusion, where intermediate noisy candidates and accepted motion history require separate update rules. PCM converts accepted state summaries, state changes, and text conditions into dynamically updated content slots, while bounded attention cache preserves recent motion features. These slots evolve with accepted motion rather than remaining static, providing dynamically updated motion context without explicitly storing arbitrary past tasks for exact recall. themselves guarantee balance or appropriate foot contact after execution. Motion generation and physical tracking can also be coupled within control framework. CLoSD uses diffusion planner with simulated feedback for multi-task character control [62], while OMG studies multimodal motion generation for humanoids [63]. In contrast, our work focuses on generating continuous kinematic references from changing instructions and constraints. These references are executed by an existing tracking system, allowing us to evaluate generation accuracy and inference cost separately from the qualitative simulation and hardware demonstrations of physical execution.

sections.title: 3 DATASETS AND RETARGETING
sections.content: Learning common motion generator from human and robot recordings requires consistent embodiment, temporal resolution, and feature representation. We combine BONES Seed [25], HumanML3D [26], and HiPHI [24] in 29-DoF G1 representation with 414 physical features at 25 Hz. The resulting training pool contains 156,819 motion records and 588.92 stored hours, including admitted mirrored records. Fig. 3 summarizes the corpus, quantifies lower-body target alignment, and illustrates stored retargeted motions. 3.1 Dataset Construction BONES Seed provides robot motion references, while HumanML3D and HiPHI contribute human motion recordings and their associated descriptions. For HiPHI, we select only the high-precision human-motion subset and exclude the object-interaction subset. We retarget the selected human body motions to G1; object trajectories and object-interaction supervision are not part of the resulting motion-generation dataset. The training pool comprises 124,658 BONES Seed records, 14,612 HumanML3D records, and 17,549 HiPHI records. We retain the source captions, mirror identities, and transformation provenance with each exported record. The validation and test manifests contain 9,998 and 12,831 additional records, respectively, and are excluded from the training pool. Counts include admitted mirrors; duration measures stored frames rather than independent capture time. The complete split statistics are provided in App. A. 3.2 Motion Retargeting 2.3 Humanoid Motion Tracking and Control Humanoid control combines motion planning with the physical constraints of balance, actuation, and contact [54]. In physics-based character animation, DeepMimic learns control policies that imitate example motions while pursuing task objectives [55]. Learning-based systems have advanced whole-body teleoperation, human-motion imitation, and expressive tracking [56], [57], [58], [59]. Retargeting methods such as GMR [60] align human recordings with robot embodiment, but kinematic agreement alone does not establish dynamic feasibility. Large-scale trackers such as SONIC [61] provide an execution layer for diverse motion references. This distinction between kinematic generation and physical tracking is important: accurate reference poses do not by BONES Seed motions retain their official G1 trajectories through resampling and representation conversion. For HumanML3D and HiPHI, we use source-specific adapters built on General Motion Retargeting (GMR) [60]. HumanML3D motions are reconstructed from AMASS [64] parameters using the SMPL-H body-and-hand model [65], whereas HiPHI motions are reconstructed using BVH forward kinematics. Rest-pose transforms and pelvis-height scaling align the human skeletons with the common robot asset. Root translations and local rotations are resampled to 25 Hz before retargeting. The solver combines position and orientation objectives under joint limits, followed by temporal refinement and bounded ground and rate corrections. App. details the asset checks and conversion procedure. SUBMITTED TO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 5 Fig. 3: Fused G1 Datasets and Retargeting Assessment. (a) Training-set composition by stored duration, including mirrors. (b) Ankle (left, logarithmic axis) and pelvis (right) mapped-target residual distributions over all 38,028 admitted human-source records; dots mark cross-clip medians. (c) Selected poses replayed from stored G1 trajectories. Metric definitions appear in App. A. 3.3 Retargeting Assessment We assess mapped-target alignment over all 18,525 admitted HumanML3D and 19,503 admitted HiPHI records across the training, validation, and test splits. For each clip, we compute the 95th-percentile distance between robot body origin and its scaled, offset human target; paired ankles use the worse side, and clips receive equal weight. Fig. 3(b) shows the ankle and pelvis distributions for the complete admitted cohorts, without selecting low-error clips. The crossclip median ankle residuals are 1.49 cm on HumanML3D and 0.93 cm on HiPHI; the corresponding cross-clip 95th percentiles are 3.37 and 2.39 cm. Median pelvis residuals are 0.99 and 0.56 cm, respectively. These statistics quantify alignment to the mapped lower-body objectives. The stored examples in Fig. 3(c) illustrate leg extension, stepping, and coordinated arm motion. Such pose-level evidence and mapped-target position residuals describe different aspects of retargeting: target offset alone does not establish loss of the depicted action, and recognizable poses do not establish precise hand contact. Separately, conversion between the stored motion formats and the 414-D representation has maximum round-trip position discrepancy of 1.31 106 over the admitted humansource records.

The streaming generation algorithm in App. B.2 summarizes the procedure. The exact cache grows only to windows, and each recurrent state and slot bank has fixed size. For fixed output window and conditioning budget, memory and computation per new window therefore do not grow with elapsed generation time. This bound concerns computational context; it does not imply error-free motion over arbitrary durations. 4.4 State-Preserving Efficient Inference Repeated diffusion denoising incurs overhead from kernel launches, intermediate memory traffic, and unnecessary state materialization. We address these costs through statepreserving execution optimizations while maintaining root body dependencies and accepted-only history updates. Read-only execution. During denoising, we avoid materializing state proposals and diagnostics that are not consumed by either the prediction or later commit. All recurrent computation contributing to predicted motion is retained. The canonical clean-history pass still constructs and commits the complete accepted state. Fusion Kernel. We fuse Mamba transition preprocessing, including the decay activation, decay floor, step-size transformation, and product iAi, into single traversal. Intermediate values remain in FP32 registers before outputs are written in the scans required layout. Compatible scale shift and gated-residual operations are also fused in the execution variants that pass the numerical checks. The attention operator and recurrent scan are retained. Exact preprocessing and precision boundaries are given in App. B. CUDA Graph replay. The root and body DiT sequence stacks use separate CUDA Graphs. Within each stack, the textconditioned, spatially conditioned, and unconditional CFG branches execute serially and are captured together. Input projections, conditioning preparation, root-output processing, root-to-local conversion, and body-input construction remain outside these stack-level graphs. Stable input and state buffers are refreshed before replay. Sampling updates, random-number handling, recentering, and accepted-state commits also remain outside capture. Graphs are rebuilt when tensor layouts or parameter versions become incompatible; unsupported calls use the reference path. Fig. 6: CUDA Graph and Kernel Fusion. Stack-level CUDA Graph replay of the three CFG branches, with separate graphs for the root and body DiT stacks, and fused Mamba transition preprocessing. 4.5 Learning Objective We optimize clean-window prediction with four terms. The hybrid term Lhyb applies Smooth L1 to explicit root patches and body latents. The decoded-body term Lbody applies L1 to reconstructed articulation. The goal term Lgoal applies L1 only to observed coordinates inside the generated window; later goals remain conditioning inputs until their target frames enter the output window. The consistency term LFK measures Euclidean disagreement between joint positions obtained from decoded rotations through forward kinematics and those represented directly by decoded position features. Each term is normalized over its applicable elements. Their coefficients are denoted by λhyb, λbody, λgoal, and λFK: = λhybLhyb + λbodyLbody + λgoalLgoal + λFKLFK. (15) The codec is frozen during denoiser training. Histories, generation regions, and future observations use explicit validity masks; outputs outside the generation region are excluded from the supervised reduction. The common budget used for architecture comparisons is specified in Sec. 5.

We then isolate the contributions of recurrent modeling and persistent content memory through architectural ablations in Sec. 5.3. Finally, we evaluate whether the proposed execution optimizations reduce inference latency without altering generated outputs or committed historical states in Sec. 5.4. Motion Mamba 2.0 is jointly trained with Mamba-3 and persistent content memory (PCM) enabled from initialization. The G1 motion codec remains frozen, while cached text features provide conditioning. Training minimizes the four-term objective in Eq. (15). We use AdamW for 100,000 updates with global batch size of 512 throughout training. The learning rate increases linearly from 106 at update 1 to 5 105 at update 500, followed by cosine decay to 105 at update 100,000. Gradients are clipped to maximum norm of 1.0. The generation length is fixed at 52 frames. History/future lengths (H, ) are sampled from (0, 0), (52, 0), (196, 0), (0, 196), (52, 144), and (144, 52), with respective frequencies of 2, 5, 4, 2, 4, 3 per 20 updates. The maximum sampled training history is therefore 196 frames (7.84 s). Training samples are drawn from BONES Seed, retargeted HumanML3D, and retargeted HiPHI in 70:15:15 ratio. Each sample contains 52-frame generation window with historical motion conditions constructed from ground-truth sequences and sampled future constraints; training does not autoregressively roll out generated histories. Text and spatial condition dropout are both set to 0.1, with an empty spatialcondition probability of 0.2. For fair comparison, all baselines and architectural variants are independently trained on the same G1 corpus under the matched 100,000-update budget and batch-size schedule. All evaluations use the resulting G1-adapted checkpoints rather than the original pretrained releases. Further details are provided in App. C. Evaluation Protocol. Motion is generated at 25 Hz in 52frame windows (2.08 s). Retargeted HiPHI [24] is evaluated over 1, 4, 9, and 19 windows (2.0839.52 s), while BONES Seed [25] and retargeted HumanML3D [26] use 1 and 4 windows. For each horizon and method, 128 held-out initialization families and three noise seeds yield 384 rollouts under paired evaluation conditions. HiPHI also shares initial histories, spatial targets, and noise seeds across horizons, while instruction schedules and terminal deadlines differ. Each trial specifies root target and one wrist or ankle target, available from rollout onset with terminal deadline; only the active text instruction is provided during generation. Sampling uses 10-step deterministic DDIM (η = 0) [77] with uniformly spaced timesteps and text/spatial guidance scales of (2, 2). Further details are provided in App. C. Evaluation Metrics. Root CE measures horizontal rootposition error in the world XZ plane, while End CE measures the 3D positional error of the constrained wrist or ankle at the terminal deadline, both in centimeters. Command matching (Cmd.) evaluates coarse root-motion state agreement. Textmotion alignment is evaluated by R@3 using independently trained, frozen evaluators for each benchmark. HiPHI uses 32 generated candidates, whereas BONES Seed and HumanML3D use one matched generated candidate and 31 fixed real-motion distractors. R@3 is therefore comparable within, but not across benchmarks. L2-FID compares distributions of L2-normalized 256-dimensional motion features from phase-paired 52-frame windows, including those in extended rollouts. Latency is measured per accepted window at batch size one. Metric aggregation and reference protocols are detailed in App. C. 5.2 Main Results Results on HiPHI. Tab. 1 compares four horizons from 2.08 to 39.52 s. Motion Mamba 2.0 achieves the lowest Root CE at every duration and the lowest or tied-lowest End CE. At 18.72 s, Root/End CE reach 2.87/8.45 cm, compared with 6.17/18.07 cm for MotionStreamer and 8.15/11.06 cm for ARDY. At 39.52 s, our method achieves 7.55/13.64 cm, reducing Root CE by 3.0% relative to MotionStreamer (7.78 cm) and outperforming the best competing End CE of 14.84 cm from ARDY by 8.1%. These results demonstrate accurate terminal constraint satisfaction over extended rollouts. qualitative comparison with ARDY under distant spatial constraint is provided in App. C.6. Motion Mamba 2.0 also achieves the highest Cmd. and R@3 across all four horizons, supporting command agreement and textmotion retrieval under the evaluated protocol. At 39.52 s, Cmd. and R@3 reach 46.05% and 23.68%, compared with 41.34% for MoLingo and 19.61% for OMG, respectively. The method obtains the lowest L2-FID at 8.32, 18.72, and 39.52 (0.401, 0.402, and 0.409); CMDM leads at 2.08 (0.337 versus 0.410), and the 8.32 advantage over DreamControl (0.402) is small. Together, these results demonstrate strong terminal control alongside long-horizon command agreement and retrieval performance. Results on BONES Seed. Tab. 2 evaluates short-horizon generation on native G1 trajectories from BONES Seed. Motion Mamba 2.0 achieves the lowest Root/End CE and highest R@3 at both durations. At 8.32 s, Root CE decreases to 1.86 cm from 4.96 cm for ARDY, relative reduction of 62.5%, while End CE decreases from 10.16 to 6.86 cm. At 39.52 s, introducing Mamba reduces Root CE from 60.00 to 9.36 cm and End CE from 64.86 to 15.54 cm compared with Minimal; corresponding singlewindow differences are much smaller. Adding PCM to Native consistently improves Root CE and End CE across the three benchmarks (Tabs. 46). On HiPHI at 39.52 s, PCM reduces Root CE from 9.36 to 7.55 cm (19.3%) and End CE from 15.54 to 13.64 cm (12.2%), while increasing Cmd. from 32.20% to 46.05%. The complete writer also improves Cmd. relative to both partial-PCM variants at 18.72 (47.11% versus 38.10% and 37.18%). Both partial variants retain better long-protocol Root/End CE than Native, supporting the utility of the underlying compressed-state-to-attention interface. On BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D at 8.32 s, the complete model reduces Root CE from 5.46 to 1.86 cm and from 6.25 to 2.17 cm, respectively. Improvements are not uniform across metrics: some short-horizon Cmd., R@3, and L2-FID scores favor other variants. All execution variants use identical frozen weights. The model generates 52-frame windows at 25 Hz with four windows of recent context. Detailed evaluation criteria are provided in App. D. Deployment architecture. The deployment comprises remote RTX 4090 server for text encoding and motion generation, an intermediate workstation for communication and interaction, and the onboard G1 controller for motion tracking. Generated motion references are transmitted through the workstation via ZeroMQ and SSH tunneling at 50-Hz transport rate, distinct from the models 25-Hz motion representation. The SONIC controller tracks the received references without executing the motion generator onboard. Interactive timing. We distinguish handoff latency from physical-response latency. Handoff latency is measured from system receipt of text or spatial command to completion of the corresponding motion reference on the GPU server. It includes motion generation, decoding, accepted-state updates, and text encoding when new text instruction requires it, while excluding network transmission and robotside processing. Physical-response latency starts at the same command receipt event and ends at the onset of sustained motion satisfying the command tolerance on the G1, additionally accounting for communication, buffering, and physical execution delays. These measurements are distinct from the cached-text inference timings in Sec. 5.4. 6.1 Motion Tracking with SONIC We use SONIC [61] to track the generated motion references in MuJoCo. sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Our current framework focuses on controllable humanoid motion generation and does not yet address object manipulation. Future work will focus on whole-body locomanipulation, coordinating locomotion with object manipulation.
